The pipeline is the same everywhere. The way we describe it is not: an
Excel mapping sheet here, a free-text derivation column there, and a SAS
program that only its author fully understands.

## Why two programs disagree

An Excel specification has three layers, but only two of them are written down:

| Layer | What it answers | Where an Excel spec keeps it |
|---|---|---|
| **Structure** | Which datasets, variables, types | Dataset and variable sheets |
| **Algorithm** | What to compute | The free-text derivation column |
| **Semantics** | What that computation means **when the data does not cooperate** | **Nowhere.** It lives in each programmer's experience |

Two programmers read the same derivation column. Both are certain they
understood it. Their programs disagree — not from misreading, but because
the specification never reached the point they disagreed on: what missing
means, what a duplicate means, how dates compare.

## yamaa: four components

| Component | Purpose | Links |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Schema | Declares the vocabulary of the specification. | [Repository](https://github.com/elong0527/yamaa/tree/main/yaml) / [Introduction](https://elong0527.github.io/yamaa/articles/schema-intro/) |
| Rules | Defines the meaning of each specification. | [Repository](https://github.com/elong0527/yamaa/tree/main/rules) / [Rules](https://elong0527.github.io/yamaa/articles/rules/) |
| Engine | Runs specifications in Python and R according to the rules. | [Python](https://github.com/elong0527/yamaa/tree/main/python) / [R](https://github.com/elong0527/yamaa/tree/main/R/cdiscbuilder) |
| Benchmark | Provides runnable specification examples. | [Repository](https://github.com/elong0527/yamaa/tree/main/benchmarks) / [Dashboards](https://elong0527.github.io/yamaa/benchmark/) |

## Language-agnostic

<div class="kicker">One specification. Two engines. One dataset.</div>

The specification is data — YAML — not code. It says nothing about how
any language computes.

- The **Python engine** and the **R engine** implement the same numbered
  rules, so they cannot read the same spec in two ways.
- `output_dataset = derive(input_datasets, spec)` holds in either engine:
  same inputs, same spec, same dataset.
- Validation runs before execution: anything the schema does not declare
  fails early instead of being silently ignored.

For a SAS shop this is the key property: the spec is reviewable by
people who never write the engine.

## yamaa: one principle

<div class="kicker">Determinism is a design constraint</div>

> A yamaa specification has exactly one execution. Where it would have two, yamaa fails instead of choosing.

Ambiguity is surfaced during planning, before it becomes a silent
difference in the output — rounding, missing value handling, duplicate
records, date comparisons.

* **For people:** the specification is readable.
* **For agents:** the rules avoid ambiguity.

## Anatomy of a specification

A real excerpt — an ADSL body-mass-index derivation:

```yaml
schema_version: "1.0"
domain: ADSL
keys: [STUDYID, USUBJID]
input:
  SOURCE: input/adsl.csv

columns:
  - name: BMI
    type: float
    label: Body Mass Index (kg/m2)
    derivation:
      compute:
        expr: "WEIGHTKG / POWER(NULLIF(HEIGHTCM, 0) / 100, 2)"

verifications:
  - unique:
      columns: [STUDYID, USUBJID]
```

No free-text derivation column. Every written item has a registered verb
and a rule behind it.

## ODM comes in as data, not as luck

Extraction from ODM XML is part of the contract, not a preamble:

- **Record order is part of the input** — readers return records in stored
  order; no engine plan may reorder them.
- **A field's type belongs to the dataset** — never inferred from one
  extract's values.
- Typed, profiled ingestion (ODM, CSV, Parquet) with explicit missing and
  verification rules before derivation begins.

What the EDC gave you is what the spec sees — in the order it arrived.

## Rules own the semantics

The `rules/` directory is normative: 35 contract files, about 1,250
numbered requirements (`REQ-####`), each fixing what one written item
means.

| Requirement | What it settles |
|---|---|
| REQ-0514 | Stored record order survives every read |
| REQ-0516 | A field's type is a property of the dataset |
| R016 family | Datetime comparisons need no timezone |

A yamaa spec is written to be **executed the same way twice**; an Excel
spec is written to be understood — by whoever happens to read it.

## Who builds the specification

A person who finds something unclear can ask a colleague. An AI agent
cannot — it writes code through the gaps instead.

yamaa moves agreement to the **planning stage**: people and agents build
the specification together, and questions get answered while they are
still cheap to answer.

- The spec leaves nothing for the coding stage to guess.
- The reviewer checks one artifact — the spec — not the program.
